utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-02-59-PT, the Prosecutor versus Darko Mrdja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. May I have the appearances, Prosecution first. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, learned colleagues from the Defence. Alan Tieger and Timothy Resch on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, assisted by case manager Skye Winner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good afternoon, sorry. Vojislav Dimitrijevic, lead counsel for Defence, and as co-counsel, Otmar Wachenheim. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dimitrijevic. Mr. Mrdja, let me first ask you whether you can hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to find the right channel in order to understand your answer. Could perhaps the interpreters repeat the translation of what Mr. Mrdja just said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mrdja, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the first time that you appear before this Trial Chamber; therefore, I'd like to introduce the Judges of this Trial Chamber to you, because your case has been transferred from another Trial Chamber to this Trial Chamber. To my left is Judge Canivell, to my right is Judge El Mahdi, and I, as Presiding Judge, my name is Orie. Mr. Mrdja, this hearing was scheduled orally as a result of a 65 ter -- Rule 65 ter meeting that was held this morning, and it was on specific request of the parties to have this hearing held as soon as possible this afternoon. This hearing has been scheduled in order to hear a joint motion for consideration of a plea agreement that has been concluded between you and the Office of the Prosecution. The motion has been filed confidentially and under seal, and before we further deal with this motion, the Chamber would like to turn into closed session for a short while to discuss a few items before we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Private session would do. Private session means that the public can still see what happens in this courtroom but cannot hear the words spoken in this courtroom. We'll now turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. We hear the joint motion for consideration of a plea agreement, a plea agreement that, according to the Rules, is required to be disclosed. I would like to go through the plea agreement at least through the main lines, in order to make sure, Mr. Mrdja, that everything is entirely clear to you. But before doing so, I would very much like first of all to verify whether it was you who signed the agreement. So if the usher would please show to you especially the B/C/S version of the agreement, pages 5 and 6. And could you then, without showing it to the public, of course. And could you confirm, Mr. Mrdja, that your signature appears on the pages 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, everything is in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I showed you a copy and not the original of the plea agreement. Another issue, but I'm now addressing the parties. There seems to be a slight problem as far as dates are concerned. If I look at the English version, but the same is, as far as I can see, true, but on other pages, for the B/C/S version, I find dates in handwriting on page 7 and 8, the 24th of July, whereas the typed text on page 8 refers to the 23rd of July. I can imagine that the explanation would be that there might have been intention already to sign this agreement yesterday, and that therefore the date of the 23rd of July still appears. Is that explanation a correct understanding of the origin of this inconsistency?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's also the view of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Then, Mr. Mrdja, I'll go with you, briefly, through the agreement. The commitment you make is that you'll enter a guilty plea on counts 2 and 3 of the indictment. Because you are guilty and because you take full responsibility for the acts described, in respect of counts 2 and 3. We'll later discuss the exact facts, but that is your commitment in the agreement. You may be -- you may remain seated. You don't have to stand up all the time, although I appreciate your --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Special respect. So your commitment is to enter a guilty plea on counts 2 and 3. And in exchange for your guilty plea, the parties have agreed that that'll make a joint recommendation that the Chamber will impose a single sentence in the range of 15 to 20 years of imprisonment. And the second part is that the Prosecution will move to dismiss, without prejudice to either party, the remaining charge. The remaining charge is under count 1, and it's a charge of extermination. Mr. Tieger, I do understand that if it says that the Prosecution will move to dismiss, that it will be done by way of an application for leave to amend the indictment so as to strike count 1 of the indictment. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Then the next issue I'd like to raise with you briefly, Mr. Mrdja, is the factual basis of the plea agreement which corresponds with the charges that have been brought against you by the Prosecution. The factual basis of the plea agreement consists, and I summarise, of the following: That an armed conflict took place in August 1992 in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that it involved the widespread and systematic attack upon non-Serb civilian population in Prijedor, and that you acknowledge that the crimes to which you intend to plead guilty were part of this widespread and systematic attack. Furthermore, that on the 21st of August, 1992, that you were a member of the Prijedor police intervention squad and that on that day, in your official capacity as a police officer, you participated in the escorting of an organised convoy of Muslim or non-Serb civilians from Tukovi and the Trnopolje camp in Prijedor towards the municipality of Travnik, that these civilians were in buses and on trucks. And that at a location along the Ilomska River, between Skender Vakuf and Mount Vlasic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the convoy stopped, at this location you and other members of the intervention squad implemented orders, actively implemented orders to separate military-aged men from the rest of the convoy, including a personal selection of men by yourself, being aware and expecting that these men would be murdered. A large number of these men, the estimate is in excess of 200, were then loaded into buses. These men were taken in two buses to Koricanski Stijene. Finally, they were ordered to leave those buses and either in larger groups or in smaller groups, they were ordered to kneel at -- close to a deep ravine and were shot and killed. The factual basis is also that you, together with the others, personally and directly participated in the unloading, the guarding, escorting, shooting, and killing of the unarmed men at Koricanski Stijene. From the context of paragraph 9 in the plea agreement, I do understand that where it says that these men that left the buses and were ordered to kneel were shot and killed, that not all of them were killed and that a small number, 12 men, survived this massacre, but that all the others were killed. This is the factual basis on which you agreed with the Prosecution, according to this plea agreement. Then the plea agreement also contains a cooperation clause with the Prosecution which does not give any specifics or details on what subjects or what cases or what other accused or what events you'd give information about. It's a general commitment. And even if the agreement would not have said that such cooperation would have -- could result in considering such cooperation as a mitigating factor, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence do so in Rule 101 under (B)(ii). Furthermore, the agreement makes sure that you are aware that the joint recommendation of a term of imprisonment of between 15 and 20 years does not bind the Chamber, who will impose sentence, and that the Chamber is free whether or not to follow that recommendation, of course, while applying the rules on sentencing of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The agreement also says that you'll not appeal the sentence imposed by the Trial Chamber unless the sentence imposed is above the range recommended by the parties. This is a usual clause in such agreements. It has never been tested to its validity by the Appeals Chamber and it's not for the Trial Chamber at this moment to express itself on that. The Trial Chamber noticed that your right of appeal was that you restricted yourself, although not unlimited, in your right to launch an appeal. Similarly, you agreed that you'll not move to withdraw your guilty plea or appeal against conviction, a conviction pursuant to the guilty plea. Then the consequences as far as sentencing is concerned, to some extent I referred to that already, is mentioned under 17 and under Rule 18 you give up in the agreement right you would usually exercise if a case would have gone to trial. I just mention a few of them. For example, that you would defend yourself, that you would call witnesses, that you would examine witnesses, that you would prepare for such a defence, that the right to remain silent, which is often invoked by those who stand trial, that by entering a different plea, of course, you give up that right. On the other hand, under 19, it says quite clearly that you do not waive your right to be represented by counsel at all stages of the proceedings. This is the -- I would say these are the main lines of the plea agreement. The agreement ends that no other agreements have been concluded between -- no additional promises have been made, no additional undertakings, understandings of agreements between you and the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Mrdja, I went through the plea agreement on the main lines. Is there anything that is not clear to you in respect of this agreement? Is there anything you would like to say adding to this agreement between you and the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, everything is clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mrdja. We then come to the point where I have to ask you whether you want to change your plea on counts 2 and 3 of the indictment as it stands at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am guilty under counts 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that you want to change your plea. I would like to ask Madam Registrar first to read count 2 of the indictment against Mr. Darko Mrdja.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 2, murder, a violation of the laws or customs of war, as recognised by Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Convention of 1949, punishable under Articles 3 and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you plead to count 2, Mr. Mrdja?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please read count 3 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 3: Inhumane acts, (attempted murder), a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(i) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you plead to count 3, Mr. Mrdja?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has now to satisfy itself that your plea has been made voluntarily, that your plea was informed, that your plea is unequivocal and has a sufficient factual basis both for the crime and for your participation therein. I have carefully listened to your answers when we went through the plea agreement. I have no further questions in respect of these issues, but would like to give an opportunity to the other Judges to ask any additional questions in this respect. We have no further questions in this respect. The Chamber notices that on the basis of the summaries of witness statements, witnesses that the Prosecution intended to call while presenting its case, that on the basis of the summaries, the Chamber will try to find whether there's a sufficient factual basis for your plea. The Chamber notices that among these summaries of witness statements, we find statements of potential witnesses that stated that you were present during the convoy and at the location of the killing of a large number of men, as we just discussed. The Chamber also notices that some of the survivors have described you, and the Chamber is at this moment able to verify at least a few parts of that description, that is, approximate age and approximate length. The Chamber also noticed that some of the witnesses described you and specifically referred to your teeth, where one or more teeth would be missing. The Chamber also took notice of a summary of witness statements in which it was indicated that as a result of investigations, corpses were found at that very place and cartridges from fire weapons. I am putting this to you because, of course, this evidence has not been presented. If, for any reason, the parties would consider that the Chamber would not have found an appropriate basis for an eventual finding that there's a sufficient factual basis, then I would like to invite the parties at this moment to give comments on what I just said. The Rules indicate that the Chamber should consider independent indicia and a lack of disagreement between the parties. It seems that there's no disagreement between the parties. What I just did is to see whether the material, as it has been presented during the pre-trial stage of the proceedings, would be a proper basis for us to consider whether independent indicia would support the plea. And I'm especially addressing at this moment the Defence, because the material came from the Prosecution, but it has not ever been challenged. Could the Chamber use these statements as independent indicia in order to answer the question whether the Chamber will find a sufficient Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. factual basis for accepting the plea? Mr. Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will be very short. I think that those evidences presented by OTP can be a sufficient basis for your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dimitrijevic. The plea has been entered by the accused. Mr. Tieger, would this be an appropriate time for an oral motion to ask leave to amend the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Contingent upon the Court's acceptance of that plea, the Prosecution would move for leave to amend the indictment to strike count 1 without prejudice from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We previously have asked you a question about what without prejudice meant, and especially what it did not mean. Keeping this in mind, your oral motion is to strike on page 4 of the English version of the indictment count 1, reading extermination, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(b) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. The Chamber is aware that, of course, it's under the condition that the Chamber will accept the plea, the Chamber would like to adjourn for perhaps a very short while to deliberate on whether we could continue this day or whether the Chamber would need more time to consider the applications and to consider the plea as entered by the accused, whether to accept it or not. Yes. We'll adjourn, presumably for not more than five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to avoid whatever misunderstanding, Mr. Tieger, the Chamber does understand well that under count 3, we are talking about other inhumane acts, and that's the crime, because it says attempted murder, which is considered to be a crime in many domestic jurisdictions. But is our understanding correct that by saying inhumane acts and referring to Article 5, under (i) that you would say that the crime is inhumane acts and that you just summarised what these inhumane acts were and that it is an attempt to murder those who survived?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If this would cause any further comments from the Defence, I'd like to hear. If not, we'll proceed. Mr. Mrdja, would you please stand. The Chamber accepts your plea and immediately enters its finding of guilt. This Chamber, Mr. Mrdja, finds you guilty of count 2, murder, a violation of the laws or customs of war, as recognised by Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Convention of 1949, punishable under Article 3 and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. The Chamber further finds you guilty of count 3 of the indictment brought against you, inhumane acts, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(i) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber grants your application for amendment of the indictment to the extent that the indictment will be amended by taking out of it count 1, extermination, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(b) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. The Prosecution is ordered to file the amended indictment so that the new indictment is available in the registry and is put on paper. Then finally, the registry is instructed to set a date for a sentencing hearing, but not after having consulted with the Chamber and the parties. We will adjourn until the sentencing hearing, still to be set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 5.13 p.m.
